title: Hosea 13:1–16
context: The LORD’s indictment of Ephraim reaches its height. Ephraim, once honored, became guilty through Baal and made images of silver (13:1–2), and the people will vanish like mist, dew, chaff, and smoke (13:3). The LORD recalls that he alone is their God and savior from Egypt and the wilderness (13:4–5), yet when they were filled they forgot him (13:6). He announces judgment in images of a lion, a leopard, and a bear (13:7–8), asks where their king is now (13:10–11), and pictures Ephraim as a child who will not come to birth (13:13). Verse 14 is one of the book’s hard places: its opening lines can be read as a promise of ransom from death or as questions that summon death’s power in judgment, and 1 Corinthians 15:54–55 echoes its language in a hymn of resurrection. Both readings are found within each tradition. The chapter closes with the east wind and the fall of Samaria (13:15–16), commonly linked with the Assyrian conquest described in 2 Kings 17:5–6. Shared ground: both traditions read the chapter as a sober word of judgment on idolatry and ingratitude. Versification: English 13:16 is Hebrew 14:1, and English 14:1–9 is Hebrew 14:2–10; this page keeps the WEB numbers.

verses.text: When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling. He exalted himself in Israel, but when he became guilty through Baal, he died.
verses.arminianNotes: “When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling. He exalted himself in Israel”. Arminian readers hear the tragedy of a tribe that once held respect and then turned to Baal; “he died” names the national ruin that followed that choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the fall of a proud tribe through idolatry, with death as the wage of covenant unfaithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions read “he became guilty through Baal” as the turning point, and both trace the judgment to Ephraim’s own sin.

verses.text: Now they sin more and more, and have made themselves molten images of their silver, even idols according to their own understanding, all of them the work of the craftsmen. They say of them, ‘They offer human sacrifice and kiss the calves.’
verses.arminianNotes: “Now they sin more and more”. Arminian readers see sin that grows as choices harden into habit, as the people make “idols according to their own understanding”, the work of craftsmen rather than the living God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the progress of idolatry, which forms gods by human skill and then bows to them. Some English versions render the closing line as men who sacrifice kissing the calves; either way it pictures devotion to the calf images. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an indictment of crafted worship.

verses.text: Therefore they will be like the morning mist, like the dew that passes away early, like the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the threshing floor, and like the smoke out of the chimney.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore they will be like the morning mist, like the dew that passes away early”. Arminian readers hear the transience of a people who have chosen what cannot last; similar images of cloud and dew described their passing love in 6:4.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment pictured in four fleeting images: mist, dew, chaff, and smoke. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that a people who turn from the LORD lose the stability only he gives, and many readers set it beside 6:4.

verses.text: “Yet I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt; and you shall acknowledge no god but me, and besides me there is no savior.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “besides me there is no savior.” Arminian readers hear the exclusive claim of the God who brought Israel from Egypt, together with a call to “acknowledge no god but me” that the people are responsible to answer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s sole claim to be God and savior, which leaves no room for any rival. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a confession of the first commandment and of salvation as the LORD’s work alone, echoing his words in 12:9.

verses.text: I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of great drought.
verses.arminianNotes: “I knew you in the wilderness, in the land of great drought.” Arminian readers hear covenant care and close knowledge: the LORD provided for Israel when it had nothing, which makes the forgetting of 13:6 all the more culpable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s personal and caring knowledge of his people, and many connect “knew” with his covenant choosing and providing. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as recalling the wilderness as a time of the LORD’s faithful provision.

verses.text: According to their pasture, so were they filled; they were filled, and their heart was exalted. Therefore they have forgotten me.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says of his people, “they were filled, and their heart was exalted. Therefore they have forgotten me.” Arminian readers see a familiar pattern in which abundance breeds pride and the people turn from the giver (compare Deuteronomy 8:11–14).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the ingratitude of a heart lifted up by blessing, and they hear the warning of Deuteronomy 8:11–14 coming true. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a warning that prosperity tempts God’s people to forget him.

verses.text: Therefore I am like a lion to them. Like a leopard, I will lurk by the path.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore I am like a lion to them. Like a leopard, I will lurk by the path.” Arminian readers hear the LORD’s judgment as personal and severe: the God who cared for Israel in the wilderness now meets them as a threat because they have turned from him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s righteous judgment portrayed in vivid animal imagery, and many hear Assyria as the instrument in the background. Shared ground: both traditions read the images as poetry of judgment rather than a separate teaching about God’s nature, and compare 5:14.

verses.text: I will meet them like a bear that is bereaved of her cubs, and will tear the covering of their heart. There I will devour them like a lioness. The wild animal will tear them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I will meet them like a bear that is bereaved of her cubs”. Arminian readers hear the fierceness of the LORD’s response to a people who spurned his love, while 11:8–9 shows that judgment is not his last word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the severity of judgment that will “tear the covering of their heart” and expose what lies within. Shared ground: both traditions read the lion, leopard, and bear together as one cluster of judgment images, without assigning each animal a separate meaning.

verses.text: You are destroyed, Israel, because you are against me, against your helper.
verses.arminianNotes: “You are destroyed, Israel, because you are against me, against your helper.” Arminian readers stress that the people’s ruin comes from their own opposition to the one who wanted to help them, not from any lack of goodwill on his part.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise trace the ruin to Israel’s rebellion against the LORD, the one who alone could help them, setting divine faithfulness against human unfaithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions read “your helper” as underscoring that the LORD’s intent toward Israel was good.

verses.text: Where is your king now, that he may save you in all your cities? And your judges, of whom you said, ‘Give me a king and princes’?
verses.arminianNotes: “Where is your king now, that he may save you in all your cities?” Arminian readers hear the LORD exposing the people’s trust in human rulers; they had asked for a king and princes, and now no king can save them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the failure of political saviors; many hear an echo of the request for a king in 1 Samuel 8:5–7, though Hosea may also have the northern kingdom’s recent kings in view. Shared ground: both traditions set these rulers against the LORD, the only savior of 13:4.

verses.text: I have given you a king in my anger, and have taken him away in my wrath.
verses.arminianNotes: “I have given you a king in my anger, and have taken him away in my wrath.” Arminian readers hear the LORD granting the people’s demand as a form of judgment, giving them what they chose and letting them bear its results.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s rule over the rise and fall of kings, even when he grants a sinful request. Readers differ on whether the verse looks back to Saul or to the quick succession of northern kings in Hosea’s day. Shared ground: both traditions read it as showing that kingship apart from the LORD could not save Israel.

verses.text: The guilt of Ephraim is stored up. His sin is stored up.
verses.arminianNotes: “The guilt of Ephraim is stored up. His sin is stored up.” Arminian readers hear guilt that has been gathered and kept on record rather than forgotten, because the people have not repented of it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see sin kept, as though in safekeeping, until the day of reckoning. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober reminder that unrepented sin is not erased by the passing of time, and that the LORD’s patience is not indifference.

verses.text: The sorrows of a travailing woman will come on him. He is an unwise son, for when it is time, he doesn’t come to the opening of the womb.
verses.arminianNotes: “He is an unwise son, for when it is time, he doesn’t come to the opening of the womb.” Arminian readers hear a picture of fatal delay: the moment for new life has come, yet Ephraim will not turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see folly in refusing the moment of deliverance, while the “sorrows of a travailing woman” picture the distress of judgment already coming. Shared ground: both traditions read the image soberly, as a metaphor for the people’s refusal to repent when the time had come.

verses.text: I will ransom them from the power of Sheol. I will redeem them from death! Death, where are your plagues? Sheol, where is your destruction? “Compassion will be hidden from my eyes.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will ransom them from the power of Sheol. I will redeem them from death!” Many Arminian readers hear a promise that the LORD will overcome death, with its taunt echoed in 1 Corinthians 15:55, where Paul’s wording differs. Others in the same tradition read the lines as questions calling death to do its work, since the verse ends, “Compassion will be hidden from my eyes”.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers are likewise divided. Some hear a promise of ransom that anticipates the resurrection hope of 1 Corinthians 15:54–55; others read “Death, where are your plagues?” as part of rhetorical questions announcing judgment, which fits the closing line and 13:15–16. Shared ground: this question does not divide the traditions, and Paul’s use can be read in its own place.

verses.text: Though he is fruitful among his brothers, an east wind will come, the breath of the LORD coming up from the wilderness; and his spring will become dry, and his fountain will be dried up. He will plunder the storehouse of treasure.
verses.arminianNotes: “Though he is fruitful among his brothers, an east wind will come”. Arminian readers hear a play on Ephraim’s name, which Genesis 41:52 links with being made fruitful, and a warning that prosperity cannot shield a people from the LORD’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see “the breath of the LORD” behind the drying wind, and many take the east wind as a picture of Assyria, though the verse does not name it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as judgment reaching even a fruitful people, with “the storehouse of treasure” plundered.

verses.text: Samaria will bear her guilt, for she has rebelled against her God. They will fall by the sword. Their infants will be dashed in pieces, and their pregnant women will be ripped open.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Samaria will bear her guilt, for she has rebelled against her God.” Arminian readers hear the capital’s fall as the result of persistent rebellion, and they read the grim final lines as a sober account of the violence that conquest brought, not something to dwell on.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s judgment carried out in the Assyrian conquest, commonly dated to 722 or 721 BC (compare 2 Kings 17:5–6), and read the last lines as describing the horrors of ancient war. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with grief and hear the call of 14:1 that follows.
